## Introduction

Think about the following:

- So, would you wear a veshti/kurta/angavastram, saree/silk
  paavade/dhaavani to college?
- When you want someone to *search the internet*, what do you tell them
  do?
- How do you show someone, a stranger, that you agree with what they are
  doing at that moment?
- How do you know where the exit is in a public place?
- Where would you stage a protest? How would you get other people to
  join in?
- If you want a whole bunch of 20-30-something people to [raise their
  arms up and spontaneously rock side to
  side](https://youtu.be/La0IJPt0t4Q)?
- And, what does "less than three" even mean?!!??

In the previous module on the Prisoners' Dilemma, we saw how we all are
engaged in *adversarial and transactional Games* with many other people,
most of whom are strangers to us. But as remarked before, the Human
Species is perhaps unique in that we are able to [cooperate with
strangers](https://fee.org/articles/book-reviews-september-2004/) and
[possess bourgeois
virtues](https://fee.org/articles/where-the-bourgeois-virtues-are-found)!!
So we are not always adversaries or enemies, and we are able to obtain
***unspoken agreement and correspondence with strangers*** and treat
them as our *honorary kin* for long term benefits.

[What use would this be? Would it be a Design Tool?
How?]{style="background-color:yellow;"}

Today, we will study **Coordination Games** and **Schelling Focus
Points**, and see how these concepts can help create better designs,
businesses, and maybe, art.

## The Stag Hunt

From Brian Skyrms' [Address at
UC.Irvine](https://sites.socsci.uci.edu/~bskyrms/bio/papers/StagHunt.pdf):

> The Stag Hunt is a story that became a game. The game is a prototype
> of the social contract. The story is briefly told by Jean-Jacques
> Rousseau, in [***A Discourse on
> Inequality***](https://archive.org/details/jean-jacques-rousseau-discourse-on-the-origins-of-inequality-among-men-masters_202206):

:::: pa4
::: {.athelas .ml0 .mt0 .pl4 .black-90 .bl .bw2 .b--blue}
["...If it was a matter of hunting a deer, everyone well realized that
he must remain faithful to his post; but if a hare happened to pass
within reach of one of them, we cannot doubt that he would have gone off
in pursuit of it without scruple..."]{.f5 .f4-m .f3-l .lh-copy .measure
.mt0}

[--- Rousseau]{.f6 .ttu .tracked .fs-normal}
:::
::::

> Rousseau's story of the hunt leaves many questions open. What are the
> values of a hare and of an individual's share of the deer given a
> successful hunt? What is the probability that the hunt will be
> successful if all participants remain faithful to the hunt? Might two
> deer hunters decide to chase the hare?

Here is brief Introduction to the [**Stag Hunt

## Coordination Games and Schelling Focus Points

Here is Julia Galef on the idea of Schelling Focus Points:

::: {}
<center>{{< video https:://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CFOQquw6hig width="560" height="400" align="center" title="" >}}
Coffee, Caramels, and Schelling Points by Julia Galef</center>
:::

<br> And here is another video on the same topic, but with a historical,
and spatial, angle to it:

::: fig
<center>

{{< video https:://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oDsePkuaL9Q width="560" height="400" align="center" title="" >}}

Schelling Focus Points

</center>
:::

Focal points can be used in Coordination Games: these are activities
where people's actions tend to organize into Patterns based on specific
default options. These actions could be:

a)  Conversation, Words, Phrases, Gestures
b)  Dress
c)  Travel / Meeting / Location
d)  Food and Beverage Choices
e)  Attention

The **Payoff Matrix** in SH is:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stag-hunt-payoff
#| tbl-cap: "Stag Hunt Payoff Matrix"
#| echo: false
#| 
library(kableExtra)
library(gt)
data <- tibble::tibble("Player #2" = c("C", "D"),
                       C = c("(R=3, R=3)", "(S=0, T=1)"),
                       D = c("(T=1, S=0)", "(P=1, P=1)")) 

data %>% 
  gt(rowname_col = ) %>% 
  tab_options(quarto.disable_processing = TRUE) %>% 
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Stag Hunt Payoff Matrix**")) %>% 
  gt::tab_spanner(columns = c(2,3), label = md("**Player #1**")) %>% 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(C,D,`Player #2`)) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(align = "center", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = c(C,D, `Player #2`))) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = c(`Player #2`))) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "grey"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = D, rows = 2)) %>% 
    tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "grey"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = C, rows = 1)) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("**Payoffs are (Player#1, Player#2)**")) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("R = Reward; S = Sucker's Payoff; T = Temptation; P = Punishment")) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("Shaded Cells are Nash Equilibria"))

```

The inequalities relating the payoffs in the Stag Hunt game are:

$$
Reward > Temptation > \pmb{Punishment} > \pmb{Sucker's~ Payoff} \\\
$$

There is in fact no Temptation at all! Rewards for C are always the
greatest!

[There are *two* Nash equilibria in the Stag hunt game]{style="background-color:yellow;"}. The CC corner is
representative of both players being **pro-risk** and cooperating for
higher reward. The DD corner is where each Player is **risk-averse** and
prefers to work by themselves and mind their own business, without
interference to, or help from, the other Player. This nomenclature, and the insightful analysis that goes with it, is due to [Reinhard Selten and John Harsanyi](../../../../materials/pdfs/2011-a-nobel-prize-for-game-theorists-the-contributions-of-harsanyi-nash-and-selten.pdf), Nobel Prize winners in 1994, along with John Nash.

The Stag Hunt is a less vindictive than the Prisoners' Dilemma and may
be preferable as a Model in situations where there is not so much of an adversarial engagement as there is a tendency to maximize gains and minimize risks, and a possible high-trust environment.

## Is it better to Die than to Kill?

What game is being played here?

::: {}
<center>{{< video https://youtu.be/GvV5h9Oy4L0 width="560" height="400" align="center" title="" >}}
The Chicken Game</center>
:::

<br>

This is the Chicken Game (CG), where it two Players *dare* each other to
"chicken out" and survive, when put in a very strong adversarial
situation.

The **Payoff Matrix** in CG is:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chicken-payoff
#| tbl-cap: "Chicken Game Payoff Matrix"
#| echo: false
#| 
library(kableExtra)
library(gt)
data <- tibble::tibble("Player #2" = c("C", "D"),
                       C = c("(R=4, R=4)", "(S=2, T=5)"),
                       D = c("(T=5, S=2)", "(P=1, P=1)")) 

data %>% 
  gt(rowname_col = ) %>% 
  tab_options(quarto.disable_processing = TRUE) %>% 
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Chicken Game Payoff Matrix**")) %>% 
  gt::tab_spanner(columns = c(2,3), label = md("**Player #1**")) %>% 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(C,D,`Player #2`)) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(align = "center", weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_column_labels(columns = c(C,D, `Player #2`))) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = c(`Player #2`))) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "grey"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = D, rows = 1)) %>% 
  tab_style(
    style = cell_fill(color = "grey"),
    locations = cells_body(columns = C, rows = 2)) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("**Payoffs are (Player#1, Player#2)**")) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("R = Reward; S = Sucker's Payoff; T = Temptation; P = Punishment")) %>% 
  tab_footnote(footnote = md("Shaded Cells are Nash Equilibria"))

```

And the inequalities that govern the Chicken game are:

$$
Temptation > Reward > \pmb{Sucker's~ Payoff} > \pmb{Punishment}
$$

and as with the PD, we have:

$$
R > (S + T)/2
$$

## Where do these Games show up?

While it may seem, cynically speaking, that everyone is playing Prisoners' Dilemma, one can detect situations where the Stag Hunt is more appropriate as a Model:

A. Prisoners' Dilemma

- Security Check-in at Airports, when travelling in a group together
- At Restaurants? Ever sat next to a noisy table?
- ?

B. Stag Hunt Game

- Classroom Group Projects <https://amyjanzwood.wordpress.com/2018/11/14/game-theory-and-environmental-problems-a-classroom-simulation/>
- Communities where tacit social contract that lets people live in peace with each other. 
- When people follow queues. This is a high-trust situation, where people reap the benefits of quick service
- When nobody goes to the party / protest because they don't think anybody else is going to the party, we are getting the risk-dominant outcome in a Stag hunt.
- Hans Christian Andersen.*The Emperor's New Clothes*. <https://americanliterature.com/author/hans-christian-andersen/short-story/the-emperors-new-clothes>


C. Chicken Game

- Sibling Rivalry, involved in family-home task ( similar to classroom projects)
- Corporate Environments where some people shirk work and others do not. E.g. at Call Centers where the "time-to-answer" is a measured metric
- Driving in the Wrong Direction, or driving a two-wheeler on the footpath
- Chicken Games often occur in politics and of course, in offices and
organizations, where co-workers dare each other to shirk from work the
longest!! 
- Here us a [*sermon*](https://ellerslie.com/the-game-of-chicken/)
on the Chicken Game. (Listen to the first few minutes for a good
description of the Chicken Game.)

## Wait, But Why?

- If we are going to *design "public behaviour"* ( an Ad, a Brand, a
  Public Policy, a method for Crowd Management, Signage...) you might
  want to think of which *Game* is involved
- What are the Actions and the Payoffs?
- Can you *design the Game* by changing the Matrix?
- Incentives are both Positive and Negative:
  - Costs/Benefits: Money, Reputation, Physical Danger, or mere
    Inconvenience?
- Some *apocryphal aphorisms* to consider: (Trying to imitate [Naval
  Ravikant](https://nav.al/) here `r emoji::emoji("grin")`)\
  - The best laws are those that ~~are easiest to follow~~ do not exist
    on paper
  - Useless laws weaken the necessary laws.
  - [Some Products are faulty, some others *de-faulty* (Schelling Points)]{style="background-color:yellow;"}
- If you are engaged in Participatory Research with Americans, why would you make passing reference to "motherhood and apple pie", or "picket fences"?
